01Selected pieces

A short listening set: 12 of the 31 pieces a human listener kept while marking 52 of a pool of 254 generations. Selection is by ear, not by score: we had ranked candidates by measurable proxies for coherence (tonal clarity, consonance, onsets on a grid, self-similarity, pitch variety), and against the listener's own keep/skip marks that composite is close to uninformative, so we stopped using it to choose. It is therefore the strong end of our output and not a sample from it. 8 were prompted with captions written for this page; 3 come from the controlled-grid split and 1 from the public benchmark split, both zero-shot. Each block states which model produced it. The other sections are not curated this way, each states the fixed rule it used.

03Same caption, seven systems

One player, seven sources. Switching system keeps the playback position, so you can flip between systems inside the same phrase, which is the only way a difference becomes audible.

How the captions were chosen. By the chord-richness of the real reference piece, a rule blind to what any system produced, taking a block from the top of that ranking. Caption 16 is included because we lose there: our output reaches max polyphony 7 against the reference's 18 while one baseline matches it exactly. Removing it would turn this into a reel of wins.

Read Δ, not chord-time. Higher chord-time is not better; distance from the reference is. Several baselines reach high chord-time by over-texturing, and one emits a fixed note count for every caption regardless of what was asked.

04Where it fails

Our weakest axis is doing what the caption explicitly asks. Across the 126 captions in this test split that name a key, the generated piece is in that exact key and mode 17% of the time. The three cases below are real misses, and they are picked to be unambiguous: keys that are not the relative or parallel of what was asked, so they cannot be excused as near misses. Roughly twice as many captions land on a related key, which is the gap between the two key metrics in the paper.

Two things this is not. It is not tonal incompetence: the pieces are internally consistent in some key, just not the requested one, and a decode-time constraint that restricts pitches and programs to what the caption names doubles both key and instrument agreement without retraining and without changing distributional fidelity. And it is not the axis the paper's main claim rests on, which is distance to the real note distribution. We show these because a page of successes would misrepresent where the method stands.

05Model-free: what each tokenizer can carry

No model at all. One real human performance is encoded and then decoded by each representation, so there is no sampling and nothing to select: the difference is what the format can physically hold.

The ladder under each arm draws every onset in the original down to where that tokenizer put it. A vertical line means the timing survived; a slant means it was moved. The beat grids lean.

The error accumulates, which is worth reading carefully. Our representation stores the raw interval between onsets on a fixed 10 ms lattice, so its error is the same at the start and at the end. A beat grid stores positions relative to a tempo, so small rounding compounds as the piece goes on: in the first three seconds it is close, and by twelve seconds it is off by more than a hundred milliseconds. That is why the first-6-s median printed above each ladder is several times smaller than the whole-clip median, and it is the reason we report the whole-clip figure in the paper.

Paper: arXiv:2608.03999 · Code: github.com/SparcAI-Inc/Agogic · Project page: yisuanwang.github.io/Agogic

All audio is synthesised from the generated MIDI with one General MIDI soundfont, identical for every clip, then loudness-normalised. Notation is engraved from the same MIDI without manual correction, so artifacts of automatic transcription in enharmonics, beaming and rests are visible and left as they are; the notation is quantized to a 16th-note grid for legibility while the audio and the piano rolls are at full timing resolution. Wide-range keyboard parts are split at middle C onto a grand staff. These examples are qualitative evidence: the quantitative claims are over full held-out sets.

This page is self-contained, with no external fonts, scripts or network requests of any kind.
